items.title: Finding the Volume of a Sphere

sections.normalized_html: What is the volume, in cubic meters, of a sphere with a radius of [MATH: \dfrac{9}{2}] meters?
sections.readable_text: What is the volume, in cubic meters, of a sphere with a radius of [MATH: \dfrac{9}{2}] meters?

sections.normalized_html:
We are given the radius of a sphere and asked to find its volume.

The formula for the volume of a sphere is [MATH: V = \dfrac{4}{3} \pi r^3,] where [MATH: r] is the radius.

Let's substitute [MATH: r = \dfrac{9}{2}] into the formula: [MATH: V|= (4)/(3)π((9)/(2))^{3}; = (4)/(3)π ⋅ (729)/(8); = (243π)/(2)]

So, the volume is [MATH: \dfrac{243\pi}{2}] cubic meters.

items.title: Finding the Radius of a Sphere Given Its Volume

sections.normalized_html: What is the radius of a sphere whose volume is [MATH: \dfrac{32}{3}\pi\:\textrm{m}^3?]
sections.readable_text: What is the radius of a sphere whose volume is [MATH: \dfrac{32}{3}\pi\:\textrm{m}^3?]

sections.normalized_html:
We can find the volume of a sphere using the formula [MATH: V=\dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3,] where [MATH: r] is the radius of the sphere.

Substituting [MATH: V=\dfrac{32}{3}\pi\:\textrm{m}^3] into the formula, we get

[MATH: V|= (4)/(3)πr^{3}; (32)/(3)π|= (4)/(3)πr^{3}; (32π ⋅ 3)/(3 ⋅ 4π)|= r^{3}; r^{3}|= 8; = 2^{3}.]

Therefore, [MATH: r = \sqrt[3]{2^3} = 2\:\textrm{m}.]
